summary: State 744c5b881ccbe554 (source level) is 7.38x faster than amdclang's build (0.1695 ms vs 1.2505 ms, 240 pairs, CI 7.374 to 7.389; static check passes, battery 98/98). Reference headroom is 40: the baseline is not memory bound, it is bound by per-iteration load latency and barriers (64 tiles x (128 + 128 one-dword load-wait iterations) and 19 barriers per tile in 2 waves per head). The winning state launches grid (Hk*G, 8) x block 1024: every workgroup scores a tile of 1024 keys with one key per thread (16 global_load_dwordx4 in flight per wait, q read through s_load_dwordx16), reduces max and sum through a two-level LDS reduction (2 barriers instead of 8 per reduction), and accumulates 16 of the 128 output columns with the tile's keys split over 64 thread groups (16 value loads in flight per wait); the 8 workgroups of a head each recompute the scores and own disjoint output columns, so no cross-workgroup communication is needed. Results meet the manifest tolerance but are not bit-identical to the baseline (summation order within a tile differs, and the tile is 1024 keys instead of 128).

friction: static_check rejects amdclang's own spill code: `scratch_store_dword off, v0, off` / `scratch_load_dwordx2 v[2:3], off, off offset:N` are reported as illegal_instruction (operand ADDR: `off` is only a memory base/offset) in 335ff2a4b67fa9a1, 6cbaba85a9bf512e, 3a821263bd3c3fc2. Either the verifier should accept scratch accesses or `source` should report 'the compiler spilled N VGPRs' as one finding instead of 20 instruction errors.

amdclang keeps the kernel within 128 VGPRs and spills beyond that, and I found no way from `source` to raise the limit (the machine has more registers and occupancy was irrelevant here: 16 waves per workgroup). 32 x4 loads in flight (128 data registers) could therefore not be expressed at the source level; a compile flag or attribute passthrough in `source` would have allowed the test.
Source-level batching of loads is not controllable: batches of 24 + 8 loads written as two blocks were merged by the compiler into one 32-load batch (3a821263 has the same listing as 6cbaba85).
`edit` with op insert at index == block length is refused ("count 1 runs past the end of block .Lft1 (8 instructions)") although the tool description says index == block length appends.

`unroll_loads` / hand restructuring of the compiled key loop to 32 loads in flight would need a rewrite of a 140-instruction loop body with renamed registers; a transform 'fuse the two iterations of a counted loop with fresh registers' would have made that test cheap.

No way to time parts of a kernel or a deliberately incomplete variant (bench needs a passing battery), so separating the score phase, the value phase and the barrier/reduction overhead had to be inferred from legitimate variants (column split 1/2/4/8). A per-phase timing or a 'diagnostic bench' for unverified states would have saved several candidates.

No scratch memory and outputs are poisoned before the launch, so partial results of several workgroups cannot be combined; splitting the keys of one head over workgroups (the split that would cut the key bytes per CU) cannot be expressed. A manifest-level scratch tensor or a second launch (two-pass kernel) would open that.

static_check warns `undefined_read` on compiler-generated code (v_writelane_b32 v88, s4, 0 as the first write of a spill register; v_mad_u64_u32 high half) in every source state: these are false positives of partial writes.

`traffic` assumes every element is read once; this kernel reads K and V once per query head and per column workgroup (G = 4, then x8 for K), so the reported tb_per_s (0.4) understates the real traffic by an order of magnitude.
lessons: attn_decode (reference headroom 40, not memory bound): the baseline runs one 128-thread workgroup per head with a 128-key tile, a one-dword load and a full wait per loop iteration, and 19 barriers per tile. Block 1024 with one key per thread, x4 loads and two-level LDS reductions gave 4.05x; more loads in flight per wait (4 -> 16 x4 key loads, 4 -> 32 value loads) took it to 5.22x.

When a workgroup cannot be split along its reduction axis (no cross-workgroup communication), split the OUTPUT instead and recompute the shared part: 2 / 4 / 8 workgroups per head, each recomputing all scores and owning 64 / 32 / 16 output columns, gave 6.51x / 7.29x / 7.38x (240 -> 192 -> 171.5 -> 169.7 us). The gain saturates at 4: what is left is the part every workgroup must repeat.

A workgroup runs on one CU, and one CU with 16 waves moved about 4 MB of key rows in roughly 100 us here (about 40 GB/s). The remaining time behaved as load-throughput bound per CU, not latency bound: adding 5 prefetch loads per key row cost 10 % (0.90x), and 3x fewer VALU instructions in the dot product (v_pk_fma_f32 with 4 accumulators instead of v_pk_mul_f32 + adds with scalar q operands) was 8 % slower (0.92x), not faster.

amdclang reads a wave-uniform input vector (q) with s_load_dwordx16 into SGPRs and uses them as VALU operands (v_pk_mul_f32 v, s, v): no vector loads for the query at all. Rewriting the dot with explicit fma accumulators lost that form and was slower.

A two-level LDS reduction over 1024 threads (32 threads reduce 32 values each with ds_read_b128, then every thread reduces the 32 partials) needs 2 barriers instead of log2(N)+2 and compiles to v_max3_f32 chains.
amdclang spills to scratch beyond 128 VGPRs, and static_check refuses scratch accesses: keep source-level load batches at or below about 16 x4 loads (64 data registers) plus temporaries.

Battery shapes (S=300, Hk=3, G=2) exercise partial tiles and non-power-of-two heads: a restructured kernel needs the masked tail paths (j < kv_len, short tile) and they passed 98/98 without bit-identity, within rtol 1e-4.

session.final:
Shipped state `744c5b881ccbe554`: **7.38x** over amdclang (0.1695 ms vs 1.2505 ms at 240 pairs, CI 7.374–7.389). It passes the static check and the full battery (98/98), and the report is recorded.

**Which case this is:** reference headroom is 40, so the baseline is nowhere near memory bound. It was bound by one single-float load and a full wait per loop iteration, plus 19 barriers per tile, in only 2 waves per head.

**What the winning state does differently (source level):**
- **Launch:** grid `(Hk*G, 8)` with 1024-thread blocks instead of `(Hk*G)` with 128.
- **Scores:** one key per thread over a 1024-key tile, with 16 four-float loads in flight per wait.
- **Reductions:** a two-level shared-memory reduction for the max and the sum, 2 barriers each instead of 8.
- **Output split:** each head is split over 8 workgroups that each recompute the scores and own 16 of the 128 output columns, so no communication between workgroups is needed.

Results meet the manifest tolerance but are not bit-identical to the baseline, because the summation order and tile size differ.

| Step | State | Speedup |
|---|---|---|
| Block 1024, wide loads, two-level reductions | `6c9b9bf9` | 4.05x |
| More loads in flight per wait | `d10e06a7` | 5.22x |
| 2 workgroups per head | `c1a91d5b` | 6.51x |
| 4 workgroups per head | `4c835acc` | 7.29x |
| 8 workgroups per head | `744c5b88` | 7.38x |

**What did not pay:**
- A 4-accumulator fused multiply-add dot product was about 8% slower than its parent (`6d1c7feb`, 6.67x over ref).
- Prefetching the second half of each key row at the machine level was about 10% slower than its parent (`acf2e58d`, 6.67x over ref).
- Putting all 32 key loads of a row in flight could not be tested: amdclang spills past 128 vector registers and the static check rejects its spill code.

The last three ideas (8-way split, cheaper dot, prefetch) each brought under 1% or a loss, so I stopped there. What remains appears to be the key-row reads each workgroup must repeat
